title: The Language of Hands
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 17 of 40
content:
Snape's right hand improved before his left.

I knew because he began stirring clockwise again without switching grip halfway through.

He knew I knew because he caught me watching.

“Your fascination with my extremities is becoming conspicuous.”

I nearly dropped the measuring spoon.

He looked at me.

I looked at him.

Then, unbelievably, color rose along the tops of his cheekbones.

I started laughing.

“Do not.”

“You said it.”

“I did not mean—”

“That makes it better.”

His expression became murderous.

I leaned against the table, helpless.

“Are you twelve?” he asked.

“Currently, yes.”

“You are impossible.”

“So I've been told.”

His own line.

That only made me laugh harder.

He turned back to the cauldron with the stiff dignity of a man betrayed by language.

We were brewing a complex nerve restorative for St Mungo's, not for him this time. The hospital had heard about our audit work and sent a request for help reproducing a pre-war formulation whose maker had died. Snape knew the recipe. I knew the modern stabilizers. Between us, we had spent three days arguing it into something better.

The potion required paired work during the final stage.

One person had to stir continuously.

The other had to add twelve ingredients at exact intervals, some no more than four seconds apart.

Snape took the stirring rod.

I prepared the tray.

“Ready?” I asked.

“I was ready six minutes ago.”

“You were complaining six minutes ago.”

“I can do both.”

“I've noticed.”

We began.

Porcupine quill.

Three turns.

Silverleaf.

Seven turns.

A pinch of crushed moonstone.

Snape's hand moved with elegant precision.

I watched the potion color change from amber to pearl.

“Now,” he said.

I added salamander blood.

The surface flashed green.

“Too fast.”

“It was on time.”

“Half a second early.”

“You cannot possibly know that.”

“I can count.”

“So can I.”

“Debatable.”

“Keep stirring.”

His mouth twitched.

The next addition required me to reach across him.

I warned him first.

“Left side.”

He shifted.

My forearm brushed his wrist.

No one froze.

That was new.

We continued.

At ingredient nine, his left hand began to tremble where it steadied the cauldron handle.

He ignored it.

At ingredient ten, the tremor worsened.

I saw his jaw tighten.

“Switch,” I said.

“No.”

“Your hand.”

“I am aware.”

“Then switch.”

“We lose the rhythm.”

“I can take it.”

“You have not practiced this sequence.”

“I watched you.”

“That is not equivalent.”

The potion darkened at the edge.

We had seconds.

I reached for the stirring rod.

Snape's hand closed over mine.

“Wait.”

His grip was firm despite the tremor.

“On my count,” he said.

I understood.

We could transfer without breaking rhythm if our hands overlapped for a full turn.

“One.”

His fingers tightened around mine on the rod.

“Two.”

We stirred together.

“Three.”

He released.

I took over.

“Counterclockwise now,” he said.

I obeyed.

He added ingredient eleven with his right hand.

Then twelve.

The potion flashed white.

Perfect.

We both exhaled.

My hand remained on the stirring rod.

His hovered close.

The moment should have ended there.

Instead he said, “Your grip was acceptable.”

I looked at him.

“Acceptable?”

“Do not become emotional.”

“I'm overwhelmed.”

“Control yourself.”

“I may need a chair.”

His mouth curved.

The teasing felt different after our hands had moved together.

Less like defense.

More like play.

That frightened me more than sarcasm ever had.

The fourth ingredient was late by two seconds.

“Stop,” Severus said.

I froze with the little glass measure in my hand. The potion's surface had gone from blue to a cloudy green at the edges. My first instinct was to add more stabilizer, to prove I could rescue the work before he lost patience.

He caught the movement. “If you compensate without measuring, we shall have an expensive bottle of speculation.”

I put the measure down.

He tested a sample in a clear dish, then compared it with the reference card we'd written that morning. The result wasn't dangerous, but it wasn't the formulation St Mungo's had requested. We could keep the batch for practice. We couldn't send it for a patient.

“That's three hours,” I said.

“Four, if you count my increasingly regrettable company.”

I looked at his left hand. His grip on the rod was tight enough to whiten his knuckles, though he hadn't complained once.

“You didn't tell me it was hurting.”

“It was not relevant until it became relevant.”

“That's a lovely definition. Completely useless.”

He glared at me. Then he released the rod and rolled his fingers open. There were faint red marks where the handle had pressed against his skin.

We took a break that cost us the batch but saved the rest of the afternoon. I fitted a thicker grip to the stirring rod, and he tested it without ceremony. He would not have thanked me for pity. He did, however, tell me exactly where the grip needed reshaping.

When we began again, we assigned the timing aloud. He called the intervals; I counted the additions; neither pretended a mistake belonged to only one pair of hands. By the final stage, the surface stayed clear.

“Acceptable,” Severus said.

“From you, that's practically a serenade.”

“Then your musical standards are as appalling as your arithmetic.”

He checked the vial seal himself, but he let me sign the production record beside him.


We bottled the potion.

Later, while cleaning, I cut my thumb on a chipped vial.

It was shallow.

I hissed.

Snape turned immediately.

“Show me.”

“It's nothing.”

His eyebrow rose.

I smiled.

“Right. I hear it now.”

“Your hypocrisy is refreshing.”

I held out my hand.

Snape took it.

Not my wrist.

My hand.

His fingers supported my palm while he examined the cut.

The contact was practical.

It still changed my breathing.

He noticed.

Of course he did.

His eyes lifted briefly to mine, then back to the injury.

“Stay still.”

“I am.”

“You moved.”

“I breathed.”

“Unnecessarily dramatic.”

He cleaned the cut with his wand and applied a drop of dittany.

The sting made me twitch.

His thumb pressed lightly against the base of mine to steady me.

Warm.

Careful.

His hands were not soft. There were calluses along his fingers from years of knives, quills, cauldrons, wands.

I had noticed them before.

Not like this.

The cut sealed.

He did not let go immediately.

Neither did I pull away.

His gaze returned to my face.

The room narrowed.

I thought he might say something sharp to break it.

He did not.

Instead his thumb moved once across my palm.

Barely.

An accident, perhaps.

Except Severus Snape did very little by accident when he was watching himself.

My pulse kicked.

He released me.

“There.”

“Thank you.”

He turned to the sink.

I stared at my healed thumb.

Ridiculous.

I was an adult. A touch was a touch. A healer might have done the same. A colleague might have.

But Snape had rules about contact.

So did I.

We had spent weeks teaching each other that touch required intention or necessity.

The cut had been necessary.

The extra second had not.

Neither had the thumb across my palm.

I looked at his back.

“Snape.”

His shoulders tensed.

“Yes?”

I could ask.

I could name it.

I could force the moment into language and watch him retreat behind every wall he owned.

So I chose something else.

“Your left hand did well today.”

He was quiet.

“Better,” he said.

“Yes.”

He turned.

There was gratitude in his face and something warmer beneath it.

“Yours,” he said, “was adequate.”

I smiled.

“Careful. Compliments twice in one day.”

“A temporary lapse.”

“I'll document it.”

“I will destroy the record.”

“Then I'll make copies.”

His eyes narrowed with familiar amusement.

We cleaned the rest of the laboratory side by side.

At the end of the night, he handed me my coat.

Our fingers touched.

The change was most obvious when I stopped looking for it.

A month earlier, every accidental touch had become an event. A brush of fingers over a jar. His hand at my elbow on the stairs. Mine hovering near his back when his balance failed but refusing to land without permission.

Now touch had begun to acquire grammar.

A palm held out meant help me up.

Two fingers against my wrist meant stop before you ruin that measurement.

The back of his knuckles against my sleeve meant move; I am carrying something dangerous and apparently words are beneath me.

One evening I found him struggling with a stopper that had sealed itself too tightly. His left hand was trembling.

“Want me?” I asked.

He froze.

I realized how the question sounded at exactly the same moment he did.

Heat climbed my face.

“The jar,” I said.

“I understood.”

“You absolutely did not.”

His mouth curved with slow cruelty. “Your phrasing was imprecise.”

I snatched the jar from him, opened it, and shoved it back.

“Fixed.”

“Remarkably efficient.”

“Say one more thing.”

He looked directly at me. “Want me?”

I nearly dropped the stopper.

His laugh rasped out before he could stop it.

That night, the language of hands gained sarcasm too.

This time neither of us pretended it was accidental.
